concepts.name: Restoring force
concepts.statement: When an object is displaced from its equilibrium position, the deformation creates a force in the opposite direction, which pushes the object back. Without such a force there is no oscillation, because the object would simply move in a straight line at constant speed.

concepts.name: Force constant
concepts.statement: The force constant tells how stiff a system is. The larger $\kk$ is, the greater the restoring force for the same displacement, and the stiffer the system. It is the slope of the graph of restoring force against displacement, in newtons per meter.

concepts.name: Hooke’s law
concepts.statement: The restoring force of a deformed system is directly proportional to its displacement from equilibrium and points opposite to it, $\kF = -\kk\kx$. This is Hooke’s law, and the simplest oscillations occur in systems that obey it. From the force and the displacement you can find the force constant.

forms.condition: small deformations, for which the object returns to its original shape

concepts.name: Periodic motion
concepts.statement: A motion that repeats itself at regular time intervals, such as a plucked guitar string or a mass on a spring moving up and down, is periodic. Each repetition takes the same time as the one before it, which is what makes a period and a frequency meaningful.

concepts.name: Period
concepts.statement: The period is the time to complete one oscillation. Its units are usually seconds, but may be any convenient unit of time. The word applies to the time for any event, repetitive or not, but here it is the time for one cycle of a periodic motion.

concepts.name: Frequency
concepts.statement: Frequency is the number of events per unit time. For periodic motion it is the number of oscillations per unit time, measured in hertz, where one hertz is one cycle per second. A count of cycles divided by the time they took gives the frequency, whether or not the count is made over one second.

concepts.name: Period and frequency
concepts.statement: If one cycle takes a time $\kT$, then $1/\kT$ cycles fit into each unit of time, so the frequency is the reciprocal of the period and the period is the reciprocal of the frequency. Given either one, the other follows at once.

concepts.name: Simple harmonic motion
concepts.statement: When the net force on a system can be described by Hooke’s law and there is no damping, the system oscillates with equal displacement on either side of equilibrium. This is simple harmonic motion, the simplest and most common kind of oscillation, and the system is a simple harmonic oscillator.

concepts.name: Amplitude
concepts.statement: The amplitude is the maximum displacement from equilibrium. It has the units of the displacement, meters for an object on a spring, and it is related to the energy in the oscillation. In one full period the object covers four amplitudes of ground.

concepts.name: Period of a simple harmonic oscillator
concepts.statement: The period and frequency of a simple harmonic oscillator depend on the mass and the force constant alone, not on the amplitude. A stiffer system has a shorter period and a more massive one a longer period. Because the period is constant, a simple harmonic oscillator can be used as a clock.

concepts.name: Kinematics of simple harmonic motion
concepts.statement: The displacement in any simple harmonic motion is a cosine of time, $\kx(t) = \kX\cos(2\pi\kt/\kT)$. The velocity is a sine with maximum $\kvmax = 2\pi\kX/\kT = \kX\sqrt{\kk/m}$, zero at the turning points and greatest through equilibrium, and the acceleration is a cosine opposite in direction to the displacement. These are the sine waves that link simple harmonic motion to waves.

forms.latex: x = X\cos\left(\frac{2\pi t}{T}\right) = X\cos(2\pi f t)

concepts.name: Simple harmonic oscillator
concepts.statement: A simple harmonic oscillator is a system that obeys Hooke’s law and so moves in simple harmonic motion, such as a mass attached to a spring.

concepts.name: Simple pendulum
concepts.statement: A simple pendulum is a small mass, the bob, hung from a light string. Displaced along its arc, it feels a net force of $-m\kg\sin\theta$ back toward the lowest point, because the tension cancels the part of the weight along the string. For small displacements it is a simple harmonic oscillator.

concepts.name: Restoring force on a pendulum
concepts.statement: For angles below about 15°, $\sin\theta$ and $\theta$ differ by 1% or less, so the restoring force $-m\kg\sin\theta$ becomes $-m\kg\theta$, and with $\ks = L\theta$ it is $-\frac{m\kg}{L}\ks$. That is Hooke’s law with a force constant $\kk = m\kg/L$, which is what makes the pendulum a simple harmonic oscillator.

concepts.name: Period of a simple pendulum
concepts.statement: Putting $\kk = m\kg/L$ into $\kT = 2\pi\sqrt{m/\kk}$ cancels the mass and leaves $\kT = 2\pi\sqrt{L/\kg}$. Only the length and the acceleration due to gravity affect the period; the mass does not, and the amplitude hardly does for small swings. This is why a pendulum keeps time.

concepts.name: Measuring g with a pendulum
concepts.statement: Squaring the period formula and solving for $\kg$ gives $\kg = 4\pi^2 L/\kT^2$. If the length is known precisely and the period is timed over many swings at a small angle, this gives the local acceleration due to gravity to several digits, which matters in geological exploration.

concepts.name: Energy of a simple harmonic oscillator
concepts.statement: A simple harmonic oscillator has no dissipative forces, so its energy is shared between elastic potential energy and kinetic energy with the total constant. The energy goes completely from one form to the other as the system oscillates: all potential at the turning points, all kinetic through equilibrium. Started from rest at $\kx = \kX$, the total is $\tfrac{1}{2}\kk\kX^2$.

concepts.name: Speed in simple harmonic motion
concepts.statement: Solving the conservation of energy for the velocity gives the speed at every position, greatest at equilibrium and zero at the turning points, with $\kvmax = \kX\sqrt{\kk/m}$. The maximum velocity is proportional to the amplitude, greater for stiffer systems, and smaller for larger masses.

concepts.name: Projection of uniform circular motion
concepts.statement: A point moving round a circle at constant angular velocity $\kw$ has a projection on a fixed axis at $\kx = \kX\cos\kw\kt$, and with $\kw = 2\pi/\kT$ this is exactly the position of a simple harmonic oscillator. The shadow of a ball on a turntable therefore moves in simple harmonic motion, and the speed and the period of any simple harmonic oscillator can be read off the circle: the similar triangles give $\kv = \kvmax\sqrt{1 - \kx^2/\kX^2}$, and one revolution gives $\kT = 2\pi\kX/\kvmax = 2\pi\sqrt{m/\kk}$.

concepts.name: Damped harmonic motion
concepts.statement: Completely undamped motion is rare, because friction and other non-conservative forces are seldom negligible; a guitar string stops a few seconds after it is plucked. For a system with a small amount of damping, the period and frequency are nearly the same as for simple harmonic motion, but the amplitude gradually decreases, because the damping force removes energy from the system, usually as thermal energy. As the damping is increased the period and frequency begin to be affected, since damping opposes and hence slows the back and forth motion, and with very large damping the system does not oscillate at all.

concepts.name: Energy removed by damping
concepts.statement: Energy removal by non-conservative forces is described by $\kWnc = \Delta(\kKE + \kPEtot)$, where $\kWnc$ is the work done by the non-conservative force, here the damping force. For a damped harmonic oscillator this work is negative, because it removes mechanical energy from the system, so the mechanical energy of a damped oscillator can only fall with time.

concepts.name: Critical damping
concepts.statement: Critical damping is the condition in which the damping of an oscillator results in it returning as quickly as possible to its equilibrium position. The critically damped system may overshoot the equilibrium position, but if it does, it will do so only once. It is often what is wanted, as in the suspension of a car or the needle of a bathroom scale, because such a system returns to equilibrium rapidly and remains there, and a constant force moves it to a new equilibrium in the shortest time possible without oscillating about it.

concepts.name: Underdamping
concepts.statement: With less than critical damping, the system returns toward equilibrium faster than a critically damped one but overshoots and crosses the equilibrium position one or more times, its amplitude gradually decreasing to zero. Such a system is underdamped, and the lightly damped oscillator whose amplitude slowly decays while its period stays almost the same is the common case.

concepts.name: Overdamping
concepts.statement: An overdamped system, curve B, returns to equilibrium without oscillating, and does so over a longer time than a critically damped one; like the critically damped system it may overshoot, but it reaches equilibrium slowly. Heavy damping is wanted where small-amplitude motion matters more than a quick return, and its cost is the slowness.

concepts.name: Finding the travel of a friction-damped oscillator
concepts.statement: When the damping is simple friction, the work it does is $-\kff\kd$, with $\kff = \mu_{\text{k}} m\kg$ and $\kd$ the total distance travelled, and the motion stops where the friction balances the force of the spring, at $\kx = \mu_{\text{k}} m\kg/\kk$. Equating the work done by friction to the change in stored elastic energy gives the total distance the object travels before it stops. This is an integrated concepts problem: friction from Newton's laws, then work and the conservation of energy.

concepts.name: Natural frequency
concepts.statement: The natural frequency is the frequency at which a system would oscillate if there were no driving and no damping force. Objects can be forced to oscillate, but they oscillate best at their natural frequency; a piano's strings sing back the note you sing at them because their frequencies match your voice.

concepts.name: Resonance
concepts.statement: Driving a system with a frequency equal to its natural frequency is called resonance, and a system driven that way is said to resonate. When you drive the paddle ball at its natural frequency its oscillations increase in amplitude with each oscillation for as long as you drive it; at driving frequencies well above or below, energy is transferred to the ball less efficiently and it responds with lower-amplitude oscillations. Radios, MRI, a child on a swing and the Tacoma Narrows Bridge are all cases of it.

concepts.name: Resonance curve and damping
concepts.statement: The amplitude of a driven, damped harmonic oscillator peaks where the driving frequency equals the natural frequency, whatever the damping. The least damping gives the highest and narrowest peak, because the damping force removes the least energy. A piano string or a radio, which must resonate at one precise frequency, needs as little damping as possible. A car’s suspension needs heavy damping, which lowers the amplitude but lets it respond over more frequencies.

concepts.name: Finding the energy a damper removes
concepts.statement: The energy a shock absorber must dissipate to damp a bounce is the mechanical energy of the oscillation, $\tfrac{1}{2}m\kv^2$ at the equilibrium position or $\tfrac{1}{2}\kk\kX^2$ at maximum displacement, and the energy a driving force must supply to raise an amplitude is the difference between two such stores. At resonance the driver puts energy in at a steady rate, so the time to reach a larger amplitude is that difference divided by the rate.

concepts.name: Wave
concepts.statement: A wave is a disturbance that propagates, or moves from the place it was created. For water waves the disturbance is in the surface of the water, for sound it is a change in air pressure, for earthquakes it is the ground itself. The simplest waves repeat for several cycles and are associated with simple harmonic motion: the gull bobs up and down as the crests and troughs pass under it, while the wave itself, the disturbance and not the water, moves on.

concepts.name: Wave velocity
concepts.statement: The wave velocity is the speed at which the disturbance moves, sometimes called the propagation velocity or propagation speed. It is the speed of the wave, not the speed at which the gull moves up and down: for water waves it is the speed of a surface wave, for sound the speed of sound, for visible light the speed of light.

concepts.name: Wavelength
concepts.statement: The wavelength is the distance between adjacent identical parts of a wave, measured parallel to the direction of propagation. The size of the disturbance, its amplitude, is a different length and is completely independent of the speed of propagation.

concepts.name: Wave speed, wavelength and frequency
concepts.statement: The speed of propagation is the distance the wave travels in a given time, which is one wavelength in the time of one period, so $\kvw = \klam/\kT$, or $\kvw = \kf\klam$. This fundamental relationship holds for all types of waves: water waves, sound and light alike.

concepts.name: Transverse wave
concepts.statement: In a transverse, or shear, wave the disturbance is perpendicular to the direction of propagation: the cord is moved up and down while the wave travels horizontally along it. The waves on the strings of musical instruments are transverse, and so are electromagnetic waves such as visible light.

concepts.name: Longitudinal wave
concepts.statement: In a longitudinal, or compressional, wave the disturbance is parallel to the direction of propagation: the cord is pushed and pulled along its own length. Sound waves in air and water are longitudinal, because fluids have no appreciable shear strength and so can carry only periodic variations in pressure; sound in solids, and earthquake waves, can be both longitudinal and transverse.

concepts.name: Superposition
concepts.statement: When two or more waves arrive at the same point, their disturbances are superimposed on one another. Each disturbance corresponds to a force, and forces add, so if the disturbances are along the same line the resulting wave is a simple addition of the disturbances of the individual waves: their amplitudes add. Most waves look complex because they are several simple waves added together, and the rules for adding them are this simple.

concepts.name: Constructive interference
concepts.statement: Two identical waves that arrive at the same point exactly in phase, crest aligned with crest and trough with trough, produce pure constructive interference: a wave with twice the amplitude of the individual waves but the same wavelength. It is one end of what superposition can do, and most real superpositions are a mixture of it and its opposite that varies from place to place and time to time.

concepts.name: Destructive interference
concepts.statement: Two identical waves that arrive exactly out of phase, precisely aligned crest to trough, produce pure destructive interference: the disturbances are in opposite directions and the resulting amplitude is zero, so the waves completely cancel. Sound from a stereo that is loud in one spot and quiet in another is the two kinds of interference at different places in the same room.

concepts.name: Standing wave
concepts.statement: Two identical waves moving in opposite directions superimpose to a wave that seems to stand in place: they alternate between constructive and destructive interference as they move through each other, and the resultant oscillates at fixed locations without travelling. The waves on a glass of milk in a refrigerator, on guitar strings and in organ pipes are standing waves, formed by reflections from the sides or the ends.

concepts.name: Nodes and antinodes
concepts.statement: Nodes are the points where the string does not move; more generally, nodes are where the wave disturbance is zero in a standing wave. The fixed ends of a string must be nodes, because the string cannot move there. An antinode is the location of maximum amplitude in a standing wave.

concepts.name: Fundamental and overtones of a string
concepts.statement: On a string fixed at both ends the longest wavelength is $\klamone = 2L$, so the lowest frequency, the fundamental, is $\kfone = \kvw/\klamone = \kvw/2L$. The overtones, or harmonics, are multiples of the fundamental: $\klamtwo = L$ gives $\kftwo = 2\kfone$, and $\kfthree = 3\kfone$, and so on. Raise the tension and all of these frequencies rise together, because greater tension means a greater $\kvw$. That is how a string instrument is tuned.

concepts.name: Beats
concepts.statement: The superposition of two waves of similar but not identical frequencies goes in and out of phase, alternately constructive and destructive, so the resultant has the average frequency of the two and an amplitude that rises and falls: it beats. Two adjacent piano keys warble and the twin engines of a taxiing jet swell and fade for this reason, and the product form $\kx = 2\kX\cos(\pi\kfB\kt)\cos(2\pi\kfave\kt)$ shows the slow cosine that carries the amplitude and the fast one that is the wave.

forms.condition: two waves of identical amplitude and similar frequency

concepts.name: Beat frequency
concepts.statement: The frequency at which the amplitude of the resultant fluctuates is the beat frequency, the absolute value of the difference of the two frequencies. It is the same for all types of waves; for sound, provided the two frequencies are similar, what is heard is the average frequency getting louder and softer at the beat frequency. Listening for beats is a very useful way to compare similar frequencies, which is how a piano is tuned against a fork.

concepts.name: Wave energy and amplitude
concepts.statement: All waves carry energy, and the amount depends on the amplitude. A wave is a displacement resisted by a restoring force, so the larger the displacement $\kx$, the larger the force $\kF = \kk\kx$ needed to create it. The work done to create the wave supplies its energy, so $\kW \propto \kF\kx = \kk\kx^2$. The intensity, an energy per unit time and area, is also proportional to the amplitude squared. Two identical waves that interfere perfectly constructively therefore have four times the intensity of one, not twice.

concepts.name: Intensity
concepts.statement: Intensity is defined as power per unit area, $\kIntens = \kP/A$, where $\kP$ is the power carried by the wave through the area $A$; its SI unit is the watt per square metre. The definition is valid for any energy in transit, including that carried by waves. It gathers the three things the energy effects of a wave depend on, the amplitude, the time and the area the wave covers: sunlight arrives above the atmosphere at 1300 W/m², and a 90 decibel sound is only 10⁻³ W/m².

concepts.name: Finding energy from intensity
concepts.statement: Because power is energy per unit time, $\kP = \kE/\kt$, the definition of intensity becomes $\kIntens = (\kE/\kt)/A$, and you can solve it for the energy, $\kE = \kIntens A\kt$, or for the time. The longer a wave acts and the larger the area it falls on, the more energy it delivers. That is why a deep-heat ultrasound treatment has a set time and a solar collector a set size.

concepts.name: Concentrating or spreading a wave
concepts.statement: Focusing or spreading a wave changes the area it covers, which changes the intensity while the power stays the same. Take the ratio of the new intensity to the old, with primes for the new quantities. The powers cancel, so the ratio of intensities is the inverse ratio of the areas. Sunlight focused by a magnifying glass onto an area 200 times smaller is 200 times as intense, enough to start a fire.

forms.condition: the same power through both areas, P' = P
